units.description: Distributions, summary statistics (mean, median, SD, IQR), graphical displays, and Normal distributions.

flashcards.definition: The arrangement of data values showing the frequency of each value or range of values.
The arithmetic average of a set of numerical values, found by summing the values and dividing by the count of values.
The middle value when all data points are arranged in order, such that half the data are above and half are below this value.
A measure of spread that quantifies the average distance of data points from the mean.
The difference between the third quartile and the first quartile, representing the range of the middle 50% of the data.

multipleChoice.questionText: Which measure of center is most appropriate for skewed data distributions?
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: Median

multipleChoice.questionText: What does a larger standard deviation indicate about a dataset?
options: Data values are closer to the mean
Data values are more spread out
The median is higher than the mean
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: Data values are more spread out

fillInTheBlank.questionText: The _______ is calculated by ordering the data and selecting the middle value.
The interquartile range (IQR) is found by subtracting the _______ from the _______.

flashcards.definition: A graphical display that organizes data into bins or intervals to show the frequency distribution of a quantitative variable.
A graphical summary that shows the five-number summary (minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile, maximum) and potential outliers.
A symmetric, bell-shaped distribution characterized by its mean and standard deviation, where data near the mean are more frequent in occurrence.
The empirical rule stating that approximately 68%, 95%, and 99.7% of data lie within one, two, and three standard deviations from the mean in a normal distribution.
The number of standard deviations a data point is from the mean, calculated as $$z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$$ for a population.

multipleChoice.questionText: Which graphical display is best for identifying outliers in a dataset?
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: Boxplot

multipleChoice.questionText: According to the 68-95-99.7 Rule, approximately what percentage of data falls within two standard deviations of the mean in a normal distribution?

fillInTheBlank.questionText: A data value with a z-score of 2 is ______ standard deviations above the mean.
In a normal distribution, about ______% of data lies within three standard deviations of the mean.

units.description: Scatterplots, correlation, least-squares regression, residuals, and influential points.

flashcards.definition: A graphical representation showing the relationship between two quantitative variables by plotting points with one variable on the horizontal axis and the other on the vertical axis.
A numerical measure that quantifies the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two quantitative variables, ranging from -1 to 1.
A type of relationship where increases in one variable generally correspond to increases in the other variable.
A relationship where increases in one variable generally correspond to decreases in the other variable.
An assessment of how closely the points in a scatterplot fall to a form such as a line, indicating how well one variable predicts the other.

multipleChoice.questionText: Which of the following values of the correlation coefficient $$r$$ indicates the strongest negative linear relationship between two variables?
In a scatterplot displaying height versus weight for a sample of adults, the points tend to rise from left to right. What can be concluded?
options: There is a positive association between height and weight.
There is a negative association between height and weight.
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: There is a positive association between height and weight.

fillInTheBlank.questionText: The correlation coefficient $$r$$ can only measure the strength of a ________ relationship between two variables.
In a scatterplot, points that are widely spread from any form represent a ________ association between variables.

flashcards.definition: The line that minimizes the sum of the squared vertical distances (residuals) between observed values and the line's predicted values for a response variable.
The difference between an observed value of the response variable and its predicted value found using the regression line.
A data point that significantly affects the position or slope of the least-squares regression line due to its extreme value in the explanatory variable.
The estimated change in the response variable for each one-unit increase in the explanatory variable, holding all else constant.
The proportion of the variation in the response variable explained by the linear model relating it to the explanatory variable.

multipleChoice.questionText: What does a residual of zero indicate about a data point in relation to the regression line?
options: The observed value equals the predicted value.
The data point is an outlier.
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: The observed value equals the predicted value.

multipleChoice.questionText: Which characteristic most accurately describes an influential point in a scatterplot?
options: Has an extreme explanatory variable value and changes the regression line slope.
Has the largest residual but lies near the mean of explanatory values.
Is always an outlier only in the response variable.
Lies perfectly on the regression line.
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: Has an extreme explanatory variable value and changes the regression line slope.

fillInTheBlank.questionText: The slope of the least-squares regression line indicates the estimated change in the ________ variable for a one-unit increase in the explanatory variable.
The coefficient of determination $$r^2$$ represents the proportion of the ________ in the response variable explained by the linear relationship with the explanatory variable.

units.description: Survey design, sampling methods, experimental design, randomization, and sources of bias.

flashcards.definition: A sampling method in which every member of a population has an equal chance of being selected, and each selection is independent of others.
A sampling technique that involves dividing the population into homogeneous subgroups and then taking a random sample from each subgroup.
A method where members from a population are selected at regular intervals, starting from a randomly chosen point.
A type of bias that occurs when individuals choose themselves to be part of a sample, often skewing the results due to strong opinions.
Bias introduced when some members of a sampled group do not respond to the survey, leading to unrepresentative samples.

multipleChoice.questionText: Which sampling method ensures that every possible sample of a given size has an equal chance of selection?
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: Simple Random Sample

multipleChoice.questionText: What is the primary advantage of stratified sampling over simple random sampling?
options: It requires less overall data collection.
It guarantees equal sample sizes for each group.
It reduces variability by accounting for population subgroups.
It avoids the use of randomization.
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: It reduces variability by accounting for population subgroups.

fillInTheBlank.questionText: In ______ sampling, every individual in a population has the same probability of being included in the sample.
______ bias can occur when participants with strong opinions are more likely to volunteer for a survey.

flashcards.definition: The practice of using chance to assign subjects to treatments, ensuring each subject has an equal probability of assignment to control for confounding variables.
An experimental design technique where subjects are grouped into blocks based on a characteristic before random assignment to treatments to reduce variability.
An experiment where neither the subjects nor the researchers interacting with them know which treatment the subjects receive, to prevent bias.
An extraneous variable that is related to both the treatment and the response, potentially obscuring the true effect of the treatment.
A phenomenon where participants experience changes in their condition due to their expectations from receiving a treatment, despite it being inactive.

multipleChoice.questionText: What is the main purpose of randomization in an experimental study?
options: To reduce the number of subjects needed
To evenly distribute confounding variables across treatment groups
To ensure a larger sample size
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: To evenly distribute confounding variables across treatment groups

multipleChoice.questionText: In an experiment, what type of design involves grouping subjects by a variable believed to affect the response before assigning treatments randomly?
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: Block design

fillInTheBlank.questionText: A ______ experiment is one in which both the subject and the experimenter are unaware of the treatment assignments.
A variable that influences both the explanatory and response variables causing a potential false association is called a ______ variable.

units.unitName: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
units.description: Probability rules, conditional probability, binomial and geometric distributions, and expected value.

flashcards.definition: The rule that calculates the probability of the union of two events by adding their individual probabilities and then subtracting the probability of their intersection.
The rule stating that the probability of the intersection of two independent events equals the product of their individual probabilities.
The probability of one event occurring given that another event has already occurred, calculated as the ratio of the intersection of both events to the probability of the given event.
The probability of an event not occurring, found by subtracting the probability of the event from one.
Two events that cannot happen simultaneously, meaning their intersection has zero probability.

multipleChoice.questionText: If events A and B are disjoint with $$P(A) = 0.3$$ and $$P(B) = 0.4$$, what is $$P(A \, \text{or} \, B)$$?
What is the probability of event B given event A, denoted $$P(B|A)$$, if $$P(A) = 0.5$$ and $$P(A \, \cap \, B) = 0.2$$?

fillInTheBlank.questionText: The formula for conditional probability is $$P(B|A) = \frac{P(A \, \cap \, B)}{______}$$.
Two events are called ______ if their intersection has zero probability.

flashcards.definition: A discrete probability distribution describing the number of successes in a fixed number of independent trials each with the same probability of success.
A discrete probability distribution representing the number of trials needed to get the first success, where each trial is independent and has the same probability of success.

flashcards.term: Expected Value of a Random Variable
flashcards.definition: The long-run average value of repetitions of the experiment it represents, calculated as the sum of all possible outcomes weighted by their probabilities.
A measure of spread that quantifies the average squared deviation of each possible outcome from the expected value.
The required assumptions: fixed number of trials, each trial independent, each trial has only two outcomes, and the probability of success is the same for every trial.

multipleChoice.questionText: What is the expected value $$E(X)$$ of a binomial random variable $$X$$ with parameters $$n = 10$$ and $$p = 0.3$$?
Which condition is NOT required for a binomial setting?
options: Number of possible successes is fixed in advance
Probability of success is the same for each trial
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: Number of possible successes is fixed in advance

fillInTheBlank.questionText: The geometric distribution models the number of ______ until the first success.
The variance of a binomial random variable $$X$$ is calculated using the formula $$Var(X) = np(1-p)$$ where $$n$$ is the number of trials and $$p$$ is the ______ of success on each trial.

units.description: Central Limit Theorem, sampling distribution of the sample mean and proportion, and standard error.

flashcards.definition: A fundamental theorem stating that the distribution of the sample mean approaches a normal distribution as the sample size increases, regardless of the population's distribution, provided the samples are independent and the sample size is sufficiently large.

flashcards.term: Sampling distribution of the sample mean
flashcards.definition: The probability distribution of all possible sample means computed from samples of a specific size drawn from the same population.

flashcards.term: Standard error of the sample mean
flashcards.definition: The standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean, calculated as the population standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size.

flashcards.term: Sample size effect on distribution shape
flashcards.definition: As the size of the sample increases, the sampling distribution of the sample mean becomes approximately normal due to the Central Limit Theorem, even if the population distribution is not normal.
Samples must be independent, and the sample size must be large enough (commonly $$n \geq 30$$) or the population distribution must be normal to justify using the Central Limit Theorem.

multipleChoice.questionText: Which of the following best describes the Central Limit Theorem?
options: The sample proportion distribution becomes uniform as sample size increases.
The sample mean distribution approaches normality as sample size increases.
The population mean equals the sample mean for any sample size.
The variance of the sampling distribution increases with sample size.
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: The sample mean distribution approaches normality as sample size increases.

multipleChoice.questionText: What is the standard error of the sample mean when the population standard deviation $$\sigma = 12$$ and sample size $$n = 36$$?

fillInTheBlank.questionText: The Central Limit Theorem ensures the sampling distribution of the sample mean will be approximately ______ when $$n$$ is large.
The standard error of the sample mean is calculated as $$\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{______}}$$.

flashcards.term: Sampling distribution of a sample proportion
flashcards.definition: The probability distribution of sample proportions obtained from all possible samples of the same size drawn from a population.

flashcards.term: Standard error of the sample proportion
flashcards.definition: A measure of variability for the sampling distribution of the sample proportion, calculated as $$\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}$$ where $$p$$ is the population proportion and $$n$$ is the sample size.

flashcards.term: Conditions for normal approximation of sample proportions
flashcards.definition: The sample must be drawn randomly and independently, and both $$np \geq 10$$ and $$n(1-p) \geq 10$$ must hold to approximate the sampling distribution of the sample proportion by a normal distribution.

flashcards.term: Role of standard error in inference
flashcards.definition: Standard error quantifies the typical distance between a sample statistic and the corresponding population parameter, which is essential for constructing confidence intervals and conducting hypothesis tests.

flashcards.term: Effect of increasing sample size on standard error
flashcards.definition: Increasing the sample size decreases the standard error, leading to a more precise estimate of the population parameter.

multipleChoice.questionText: Which condition must be met to use a normal approximation for the sampling distribution of a sample proportion?
options: Sample size $$n$$ must be less than 10.
Both $$np$$ and $$n(1-p)$$ must be at least 10.
No conditions are required to use normal approximation.
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: Both $$np$$ and $$n(1-p)$$ must be at least 10.

multipleChoice.questionText: If the population proportion $$p = 0.4$$ and the sample size is $$n = 100$$, what is the standard error of the sample proportion?

fillInTheBlank.questionText: The formula for the standard error of a sample proportion is $$\sqrt{\frac{______ (1 - ______)}{n}}$$.
To apply the Central Limit Theorem for sample proportions, one commonly requires both $$np$$ and $$n(1-p)$$ to be ______ or greater.

units.description: Confidence intervals and significance tests for one and two proportions; Type I and II errors.

flashcards.term: Confidence interval for a population proportion
flashcards.definition: An interval estimate that provides a range of plausible values for a population proportion based on sample data and a specified confidence level.

flashcards.term: Standard error of a sample proportion
flashcards.definition: The estimated standard deviation of the sampling distribution of a sample proportion, calculated as $$\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}$$ where $$\hat{p}$$ is the sample proportion and $$n$$ is the sample size.

The number of standard errors to extend from the sample statistic to create a confidence interval; determined by the desired confidence level and corresponding to the quantiles of the standard normal distribution.

flashcards.term: Validity conditions for inference about a proportion
flashcards.definition: Requirements that the sample must be a random sample, the observations are independent, and the sample size is large enough so that both $$np$$ and $$n(1-p)$$ are at least 10 to use normal approximation methods.
The long-run proportion of confidence intervals constructed in the same way from repeated samples that will contain the true population parameter.

multipleChoice.questionText: Which of the following best describes the meaning of a 95% confidence interval for a population proportion?
options: There is a 95% chance that the population proportion lies within this interval.
95% of the sample data fall within this interval.
If we repeated the sampling process many times, approximately 95% of the constructed intervals would contain the true population proportion.
The sample proportion is 95% likely to be in this interval.
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: If we repeated the sampling process many times, approximately 95% of the constructed intervals would contain the true population proportion.

multipleChoice.questionText: What is the formula for the standard error of the sample proportion $$\hat{p}$$?
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: $$\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}$$

fillInTheBlank.questionText: The critical value used to construct a 99% confidence interval from a standard normal distribution is approximately ______.
To satisfy the validity condition for inference about a proportion, the expected number of successes and failures in the sample must both be at least ______.

flashcards.term: Null hypothesis for a test about one proportion
flashcards.definition: A statement that the population proportion equals a specified value, typically denoted as $$H_0: p = p_0$$, serving as the baseline assumption for significance testing.
The mistake made when rejecting a true null hypothesis; the probability of making this error is denoted by the significance level $$\alpha$$.
Failing to reject a false null hypothesis; the probability of this error is denoted by $$\beta$$ and depends on the true population parameter and test conditions.

flashcards.term: Test statistic for a hypothesis test about one proportion
flashcards.definition: A standardized value computed as $$z = \frac{\hat{p} - p_0}{\sqrt{\frac{p_0 (1-p_0)}{n}}}$$ that indicates how far the sample proportion is from the null value in units of standard error.

The probability, assuming the null hypothesis is true, of observing a test statistic as extreme or more extreme than the one calculated from the sample data; used to assess strength of evidence against $$H_0$$.

multipleChoice.questionText: In a test about a population proportion, what does the p-value represent?
options: The probability that the null hypothesis is true.
The probability of obtaining the observed sample proportion under the alternative hypothesis.
The probability of observing a test statistic as extreme as the one calculated if the null hypothesis is true.
The proportion of times the null hypothesis will be rejected in repeated samples.
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: The probability of observing a test statistic as extreme as the one calculated if the null hypothesis is true.

multipleChoice.questionText: Which of the following describes a Type I error?
options: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis.
Failing to reject a true alternative hypothesis.
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: Rejecting a true null hypothesis.

fillInTheBlank.questionText: In the formula for the test statistic $$z = \frac{\hat{p} - p_0}{\sqrt{\frac{p_0 (1-p_0)}{n}}}$$, $$p_0$$ represents the ______.
The probability of making a Type II error is denoted by ______.

units.description: t-distributions, confidence intervals, and hypothesis tests for one sample mean and two means.

flashcards.definition: A probability distribution used when estimating population parameters when the sample size is small and population standard deviation is unknown, characterized by heavier tails than the normal distribution.
The parameter that influences the shape of the t-distribution, calculated as the sample size minus one for a single sample mean.
An interval estimate of a population mean constructed using a sample mean, sample standard deviation, and the appropriate t critical value.
Conditions including independence of observations, random sampling, and approximate normality of the population distribution or large sample size for validity of inference.
A standardized value calculated as $$ t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s / \sqrt{n}} $$ used to test hypotheses about a population mean.

multipleChoice.questionText: Which of the following best describes the shape of the Student’s t-distribution as the degrees of freedom increase?
options: It becomes more skewed to the right
It approaches the standard normal distribution
It becomes more peaked and narrower
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: It approaches the standard normal distribution

multipleChoice.questionText: Which condition is NOT necessary for performing a one-sample t-test about a mean?
options: Population distribution must be approximately normal if the sample size is small
Population standard deviation must be known
Data must be from a random sample or randomized experiment
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: Population standard deviation must be known

fillInTheBlank.questionText: The critical value $$ t^* $$ used in a one-sample t-interval depends on the sample size through the ______.
For a one-sample t-confidence interval, the margin of error formula is $$ t^* \times \frac{______}{\sqrt{n}} $$.

flashcards.definition: A hypothesis test used to compare the means of two independent populations when variances are unknown and samples are small or moderate size.
Approaches differ by whether population variances are assumed equal (pooled) or not (unpooled); unpooled is more general and common when variances are unknown.

flashcards.term: Degrees of freedom for two-sample t-test (unpooled)
flashcards.definition: A calculated approximation often using the Welch-Satterthwaite equation to account for different sample variances and sizes.
An interval estimating the difference between two population means, constructed using sample means, sample standard deviations, and the appropriate t critical value.
Include independent random samples from each population, independence between samples, and normality of each population or sufficiently large samples for validity.

multipleChoice.questionText: Which of the following is an assumption specific to two-sample t-tests comparing means that is not required for the one-sample t-test?
options: Independence of observations within each sample
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: Independence between the two samples

multipleChoice.questionText: When the variances of two populations are unknown and unequal, which formula is typically used to estimate the degrees of freedom for the two-sample t-test?
options: Student's t-distribution with $$ n_1 + n_2 - 2 $$ degrees of freedom
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: Welch-Satterthwaite approximation

fillInTheBlank.questionText: The standard error for the difference of two independent sample means used in the two-sample t-test is calculated as $$ \sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{______}{n_2}} $$.
options: sample variance of the second sample
sample mean of the first sample
fillInTheBlank.correctAnswer: sample variance of the second sample

fillInTheBlank.questionText: In a two-sample t-confidence interval, the degrees of freedom for the t-distribution are often approximated by the ______ formula.

units.description: Chi-square goodness of fit, homogeneity, and independence tests; expected counts.

flashcards.definition: A statistical procedure used to determine whether observed categorical data frequencies differ significantly from expected frequencies under a specified theoretical distribution.
The theoretical frequencies calculated under the null hypothesis, representing the number of occurrences expected in each category if the model fits the data well.
The assumption that the observed categorical data follow a specified distribution or pattern with no significant deviation.

flashcards.term: Degrees of freedom for goodness-of-fit test
flashcards.definition: Calculated as the number of categories minus one, reflecting the number of independent values that can vary in the calculation of the test statistic.
A summation over all categories of the squared difference between observed and expected counts divided by the expected counts: $$\chi^2 = \sum \frac{(O - E)^2}{E}$$.

multipleChoice.questionText: In a chi-square goodness-of-fit test with 5 categories, what are the degrees of freedom?
Which of the following best describes the expected counts in a chi-square test?
options: Frequencies predicted by the null hypothesis
Residuals between observed and expected values
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: Frequencies predicted by the null hypothesis

fillInTheBlank.questionText: The chi-square test statistic measures the total squared difference between observed and ______ counts, scaled by the expected counts.
The null hypothesis in a chi-square goodness-of-fit test states that the observed data follow a ______ distribution.

flashcards.definition: A statistical test used to determine whether the distribution of a categorical variable is the same across two or more independent populations.
A test that evaluates whether there is a significant association between two categorical variables in a single population.
Requirements including independence of observations, sample size sufficiently large so that all expected counts are at least 5, and categorical data type to ensure reliable test results.

flashcards.term: Calculating expected counts in a two-way table
flashcards.definition: Found by multiplying the row total and column total for each cell and dividing by the overall sample size: $$E = \frac{(\text{row total})(\text{column total})}{\text{grand total}}$$.

flashcards.term: Degrees of freedom for chi-square test of independence
flashcards.definition: Calculated as $$ (\text{number of rows} - 1) \times (\text{number of columns} - 1) $$ reflecting the number of independent comparisons.

multipleChoice.questionText: What is the formula for expected counts in a cell for a chi-square test of independence?
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: (row total × column total) ÷ grand total

multipleChoice.questionText: Which condition must be met for valid chi-square tests?
options: All expected counts are at least 5
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: All expected counts are at least 5

fillInTheBlank.questionText: In a chi-square test of homogeneity, we compare ______ distributions of a categorical variable across different populations.
The degrees of freedom for a chi-square test of independence is calculated by multiplying the number of rows minus one by the number of ______ minus one.

units.description: Inference for slope of regression line, confidence intervals, and t-test for slope.

flashcards.term: Slope of the least-squares regression line
flashcards.definition: The rate at which the predicted response variable changes for each one-unit increase in the explanatory variable, calculated to minimize the sum of squared residuals.
A range of plausible values for the true slope parameter of the population regression line, constructed using the estimated slope and its standard error with a t-distribution.

flashcards.term: Standard error of the slope estimate
flashcards.definition: A measure of the average amount by which the estimated slope varies from the true slope due to sampling variability.
A hypothesis test that assesses whether the population slope differs from zero, indicating a linear relationship between explanatory and response variables.

flashcards.term: Degrees of freedom in regression inference
flashcards.definition: The number of independent pieces of information available to estimate the variability of the slope, calculated as one less than the sample size.

multipleChoice.questionText: What does it mean if the 95% confidence interval for the slope of a regression line does not contain zero?
options: The relationship between variables is not linear
The slope is not statistically significantly different from zero
There is evidence of a significant linear relationship between variables
The standard error of the slope is zero
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: There is evidence of a significant linear relationship between variables

multipleChoice.questionText: Which quantity is used as the denominator in the test statistic for the t-test on the slope?
options: Sample variance of the explanatory variable
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: Standard error of the slope

fillInTheBlank.questionText: When constructing a $$100(1-\alpha)\%$$ confidence interval for the slope $$\beta$$, the critical value comes from a ______ distribution.
The test statistic for testing $$H_0: \beta=0$$ is calculated as $$t=\frac{\hat{\beta}-0}{SE_{\hat{\beta}}}$$, where $$SE_{\hat{\beta}}$$ stands for ______.

flashcards.definition: Evaluating the p-value obtained from the t-test to decide whether there is sufficient evidence to conclude a linear association exists between the variables.

flashcards.term: Assumptions for inference on regression slope
flashcards.definition: Conditions including linearity, independence, normality of residuals, and equal variance that must hold for the validity of slope inference.
Differences between observed values and predicted values from the regression line, used to check model assumptions and goodness of fit.

flashcards.term: Effect of sample size on slope inference
flashcards.definition: Larger samples generally yield smaller standard errors and more precise confidence intervals for the slope, enhancing the power of the hypothesis test.

flashcards.term: Interpretation of a non-significant slope test
flashcards.definition: Concluding that the data do not provide sufficient evidence to claim a linear relationship exists between the explanatory and response variables.

multipleChoice.questionText: Which condition is necessary to perform valid inference for the slope of a regression line?
options: The explanatory variable must be categorical
Residuals should be approximately normally distributed
Sample size must be less than 10
Regression line must pass through the origin
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: Residuals should be approximately normally distributed

multipleChoice.questionText: If the p-value of a t-test for slope is 0.12, what conclusion is appropriate at the 0.05 significance level?
options: Reject the null hypothesis; slope is significantly different from zero
Fail to reject the null hypothesis; insufficient evidence to conclude slope differs from zero
Accept that the slope equals zero
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: Fail to reject the null hypothesis; insufficient evidence to conclude slope differs from zero

fillInTheBlank.questionText: One of the key assumptions for inference about the slope is that the residuals are ______ with constant variance and roughly normal distribution.
Increasing the sample size will generally ______ the width of the confidence interval for the slope.
